label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
claim: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
scope: fishes (plaice, haddock) and humans

label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claim: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
scope: Arizona climate, 1390s–1910s, inferred from ponderosa (yellow) pine rings

label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
claim: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.
quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells
scope: growing cells of plants and animals, especially plant elongation and early embryos

label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claim: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
scope: brine-shrimps (Artemia) in waters of varying salinity

label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis
claim: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
quote: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.
scope: growth of organisms generally

label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claim: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
quote: We may take it, then, as an established fact, whose full extent and bearings are still awaiting investigation, that there exist substances both within and without the organism which have a marvellous power of accelerating growth, and of doing so in such a way as to affect not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
scope: animals (tadpoles, mammals, birds), with parallels in plants

label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them
claim: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
quote: And we then, I think, draw near to the conclusion that what is true of these is universally true, and that the great function of natural selection is not to originate, but to remove
scope: evolution of organic form generally

label: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claim: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.
quote: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.
scope: regenerating tadpole tails, possibly regeneration generally

label: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claim: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.
quote: A complete curve of growth, starting from zero, has the same essential characteristics as the regeneration curve.
scope: regenerating tissues and whole-organism growth

label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claim: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.
quote: It depends upon the respective rates of growth, upon a ratio between the rate of regeneration and the rate of growth of the uninjured limb
scope: Crustacea with asymmetric claws (lobster, Alpheus, crabs)

label: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration
claim: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.
quote: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”
scope: worms and worm-like animals that reproduce by fission

label: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases
claim: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising superficial resistance.
quote: I take it that the sudden arrest of velocity is much more likely to be due to a sudden increase of resistance than to a sudden diminution of internal energies: in other words, I suspect that it is coincident with some notable event of histological differentiation, such as the rapid formation of a comparatively firm skin
scope: growing organisms generally, including regenerating tissues

label: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claim: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.
quote: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.
scope: ontogeny and phylogeny of organic form

label: Cell structure matters only as the visible expression of forces and energy
claim: The study of visible cell structure has little value except as part of a dynamical investigation, because the activities of a cell are due to energy and forces, not to particular material particles or structures as such.
quote: In short it would seem evident that, except in relation to a dynamical investigation, the mere study of cell structure has but little value of its own.
scope: cells generally, including germ-cells and ova

label: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction
claim: The spindle and asters of dividing cells are lines of force of a bipolar field made visible by more permeable particles, like iron filings between magnet poles, and they cannot be explained by mere mechanical traction on a protoplasmic web but require some polarised and polarising force analogous to magnetism or electricity.
quote: any explanation which is based, like Rhumbler’s, on mere mechanical traction, is obviously inadequate, and we shall find ourselves limited to the hypothesis of some polarised and polarising force, such as we deal with, for instance, in the phenomena of magnetism or electricity.
section: Spindle and asters as lines of force
scope: caryokinetic (mitotic) division of animal and plant cells

label: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension
claim: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.
quote: So long as the fluid substance of the nucleus is qualitatively different from, and incapable of mixing with, the fluid or semi-fluid protoplasm which surrounds it, we shall expect it to be, as it almost always is, of spherical form.
scope: nuclei of cells generally; contrasted with muscle and epithelial cells with stiffened cytoplasm

label: Morphological polarity of the cell is the outward sign of a dynamical polarity
claim: The visible polarity of a cell (symmetry of structure about an axis, such as nucleus–centrosome or free–attached surface) is the outward expression of a real polarised distribution of forces, whose lines of force are made visible where particles of matter become strung together under those forces.
quote: The _morphological_ “polarity” is accompanied by, and is but the outward expression (or part of it) of a true _dynamical_ polarity, or distribution of forces; and the “lines of force” are rendered visible by concatenation of particles of matter, such as come under the influence of the forces in action.
scope: cells with recognisable axes of symmetry, e.g. ova, columnar and ciliated epithelial cells

label: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth
claim: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.
quote: This phenomenon is nothing else than what we call in ordinary language, a “froth” or a “foam.” It is a surface-tension phenomenon, due to the interacting surface-tensions of two intermixed fluids, not very different in density, as they strive to separate.
scope: nuclear and cytoplasmic alveolar meshworks of cells

label: Fine internal networks and granules seen in fixed cells are largely artefacts
claim: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present in the living cell.
quote: While this assumption is reasonable and justified as regards the general outward form of small organisms or of individual cells, enough has been done of late years to shew that the case is totally different in the case of the minute internal networks, granules, etc., which represent the alleged _structure_ of protoplasm.
scope: histological preparations of cells fixed with chemical reagents

label: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane
claim: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the equatorial plane.
quote: the fact is that the chromatin substance now _behaves_ after the fashion of a “diamagnetic” body, and is repelled from the stronger to the weaker parts of the field.
section: Nucleus and chromatin in the field
scope: nuclei and chromosomes of dividing cells

label: Differences of electric potential play a great part in cell division
claim: Differences of electric potential between cell constituents, and between parts of the egg, play a great part in cell division; the potential difference between animal and vegetative poles of a fertilised egg fluctuates or reverses at successive segmentations, and the electrical difference of chromatin is greatest at mitosis.
quote: Among other investigations, all leading towards the same general conclusion, namely that differences of electric potential play a great part in the phenomenon of cell division
scope: dividing cells and fertilised eggs (e.g. Fundulus, toad, turtle)

label: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces
claim: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.
quote: in all cells whatsoever, the process of division must somehow be explained as the result of a conflict between surface-tension and its opposing forces.
scope: all dividing cells

label: Entry of the first spermatozoon raises the surface tension of the egg
claim: Because later spermatozoa fail to enter the egg after the first, an immediate consequence of sperm entry is an increase in the surface tension of the egg.
quote: other spermatozoa, subsequent to the first, fail to effect an entry, we may safely conclude that an immediate consequence of the entry of the spermatozoon is an increase in the surface-tension of the egg
scope: fertilisation of animal eggs

label: The pronuclei travel curved paths and meet before reaching the centre of the egg
claim: Given an attraction between the male and female pronuclei and a force drawing them toward the egg centre, their paths lie within the triangle formed by the two bodies and the centre, are curved (convex toward the line joining them) unless they start on a diameter, and the pronuclei meet a little before the centre and then travel straight to it.
quote: (2) unless the two bodies happen to lie, to begin with, precisely on a diameter of the cell, their paths until they meet one another will be curved paths, the convexity of the curve being towards the straight line joining the two bodies; (3) the two bodies will meet a little before they reach the centre;
scope: pronuclear migration in fertilised eggs (e.g. frog)

label: Mitotic phenomena follow from simple physical assumptions and have secondary significance
claim: Most if not all of the intracellular phenomena of mitosis follow inevitably from very simple assumptions about the physical constitution of the cell and a simple distribution of polarised forces within it, and are likely to prove of only remote and secondary biological significance.
quote: Most, if not all of them, would seem to follow immediately and inevitably from very simple assumptions as to the physical constitution of the cell, and from an extremely simple distribution of polarised forces within it.
scope: intracellular phenomena of cell division in plants and animals

label: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
claim: Although chromosome number is constant within a species, the range of numbers across plants and animals is small: few organisms have fewer than six chromosomes in the germ-nuclei and fewer still have more than sixteen.
quote: (as regards the germ-nuclei) few organisms have less than six chromosomes, and fewer still have more than sixteen
scope: germ-nuclei (haploid chromosome number) of plants and animals

label: Details of mitosis vary among close relatives and are not specific to the organism
claim: The details of mitosis (presence of visible caryokinesis, position of the field of force, number of chromosome groups, chromosome form and arrangement) vary greatly even among closely related organisms or within one species, and are not specifically related to the organism in which they occur.
quote: there seem to be strong grounds for believing that these and many similar phenomena are in no way specifically related to the particular organism in which they have been observed, and are not even specially and indisputably connected with the organism as such.
scope: mitosis in plants and animals, e.g. Copepods, Ascaris megalocephala

label: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification
claim: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of the systematist.
quote: But we have little right to expect, and in point of fact we shall very seldom and (as it were) only accidentally find, that these embryological categories coincide with the lines of “natural” or “phylogenetic” classification which have been arrived at by the systematic zoologist.
scope: early embryonic development of animals

label: Surface tension gives the cell its outline and morphological individuality
claim: The cell is a sphere of action of localised forces, of which surface tension gives the cell its outline and individuality; partial versus total segmentation of eggs, and unicellular versus multicellular organisation, differ in whether surface tensions succeed in forming visible separations between cells.
quote: surface-tension is the particular force which is especially responsible for giving to the cell its outline and its morphological individuality.
section: The cell as a sphere of action
scope: cells, segmenting eggs, Infusoria and small Turbellaria

label: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body
claim: The centrosome is essentially a dynamic centre of force, which may or may not consist of a visible concentration of matter but tends to produce one, as shown by cells that live without visible centrosomes and centrosomes that disappear and form anew.
quote: We may safely take it that the centrosome, or the “attraction sphere,” is essentially a “centre of force,” and that this dynamic centre may or may not be constituted by (but will be very apt to produce) a concrete and visible concentration of matter.
scope: centrosomes of animal and plant cells

label: A continuous field of force shapes the whole organism regardless of its cells
claim: The multicellular organism is not a colony of independent cells: a continuous field of force runs through the entire organism, not restricted to protoplasmic continuity, and shapes it independently of the number, size and form of its cells.
quote: And such a continuous field of force, somehow shaping the whole organism, independently of the number, magnitude and form of the individual cells, which enter, like a froth, into its fabric, seems to me certainly and obviously to exist.
scope: multicellular plants and animals

label: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claim: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.
quote: So far then, as growth goes on, unaffected by pressure or other external force, the fluidity of protoplasm, its mobility internal and external, and the manner in which particles move with comparative freedom from place to place within, all manifestly tend to the production of swelling, rounded surfaces, and to their great predominance over plane surfaces in the contour of the organism.
section: Growth by imbibition versus crystal growth
scope: living cells and organisms growing free of external pressure, contrasted with crystals

label: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claim: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.
quote: Among the forces which determine the forms of cells, whether they be solitary or arranged in contact with one another, this force of surface-tension is certainly of great, and is probably of paramount importance.
section: Surface tension and the forms of cells
scope: all cells, solitary or in aggregates

label: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claim: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.
quote: Such symmetry is in a high degree characteristic of organic forms, and is rarely absent in living things,—save in such cases as amoeba, where the equilibrium on which symmetry depends is likewise lacking.
scope: organic forms generally, especially cells

label: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claim: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.
quote: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension
section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
scope: naked protoplasm, amoeboid cells and pseudopodia

label: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claim: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.
quote: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension
section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
scope: slime-mould plasmodia and amoeboid organisms

label: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claim: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.
quote: In the case of the naked protoplasmic cell, as the amoeboid phase is emphatically a phase of freedom and activity, of chemical and physiological change, so, on the other hand, is the spherical form indicative of a phase of rest or comparative inactivity.
section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
scope: naked protoplasmic cells, amoebae and other protists with resting stages

label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claim: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.
quote: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly
section: Budding yeast and localised tension changes
scope: budding yeast cells

label: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claim: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.
quote: The little organism as a whole is not a figure of equilibrium or of minimal area; but each new bud or separate chamber is such a figure, conditioned by the forces of surface tension, and superposed upon the complex aggregate of similar bubbles after these latter have become consolidated one by one into a rigid system.
scope: multichambered foraminifera, desmids and other organisms formed by successive stages of growth and consolidation

label: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claim: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.
quote: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.
scope: organisms and cells across sizes

label: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
claim: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.
quote: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist
section: Plateau's surfaces of revolution in cells
scope: unicellular organisms and cells of simple aggregates

label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claim: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.
quote: the normal height of the spherical cap over the end of the cylindrical cell is just a very little more than one-eighth of the diameter of the cylinder, or of the radius of the sphere. And these are the proportions which we recognise, under normal circumstances, in such a case as the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra where its free end is capped by a portion of a sphere.
scope: cylindrical cells with free spherical ends, e.g. Spirogyra and other filamentous algae

label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claim: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.
quote: But this liquid cylinder has its limit of stability when its length equals its own circumference, and therefore just at the points so defined it tends to disrupt into separate segments
section: Instability of liquid cylinders and beading
scope: viscid capture threads of orb-weaving spiders; liquid films on fibres

label: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claim: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.
quote: In the case of the hydroid calycle (Fig. 72), we are led to the conclusion that the two common and conspicuous features of notching or indentation of the cup, and of constriction or annulation of the long cylindrical stem, are phenomena of the same order and are due to surface-tension in both cases alike.
scope: calycles and stems of campanularian hydroids and other small organic cups

label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claim: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.
quote: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.
scope: elongated plant cells, algae, yeasts and other walled cells grown free of external restraint

label: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claim: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.
quote: To the fact that these little organisms belong to an order of magnitude in which form is mainly, if not wholly, conditioned and controlled by molecular forces, is due the limited range of forms which they actually exhibit.
section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
scope: unicellular organisms, bacteria, spores and free cells

label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claim: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.
quote: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_
section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
scope: bacteria and micrococci

label: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claim: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.
quote: The cups of the various species of Vorticella (Fig. 75) are nothing in the world but a beautiful series of unduloids, or partial unduloids, in every gradation from a form that is all but cylindrical to one that is all but a perfect sphere.
scope: Vorticella and other cup-shaped or flask-shaped ciliates and flagellates

label: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claim: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a protective purpose, explains their form.
quote: that this surface pellicle or membrane was inevitably bound, by molecular forces, to become a surface of the least possible area which the circumstances permitted
scope: loricate protozoa such as Salpingoeca, Tintinnus, Dinobryon and Codonella
